# Electrical - Low beams out, high beams still work

When a vehicle's lighting system presents a split failure where low beams are dead but high beams and parking lights function correctly, the diagnostic path is often more nuanced than a simple fuse or bulb swap. In the specific case of a 2001 Mitsubishi Lancer CE, the symptoms point toward a logic conflict within the headlight switch assembly rather than a downstream component failure. The fact that you can hear the relay clicking when attempting to engage the low beams confirms that the stalk switch is sending a valid request signal to the control circuit. If the switch were internally open or disconnected, the relay coil would not energize, and no click would occur.

The diagnostic data providedâspecifically the voltage readings on the three terminals at the headlight connectorâis the critical pivot point for this diagnosis. When in low beam mode, all three terminals read +12V. This indicates that the power feed is reaching the harness correctly, but the load (the bulb) is not receiving the specific signal to complete the circuit. Conversely, when switching to high beams, one terminal drops to 0V. This behavior reveals how the lighting logic operates: the switch likely uses a common ground strategy or a switched positive logic where the high beam mode changes the state of the control pin relative to the low beam state.

The most telling symptom emerges during the transition between modes. The high beam toggle no longer acts as a latching switch; it only illuminates while physically held down. This is a classic sign of an internal contact failure within the rotary or lever mechanism of the headlight stalk. In these specific automotive switches, there are often multiple contacts: one for the parking light circuit, one for the low beam ground/positive logic, and a separate high beam toggle. When the internal wiper arm or spring-loaded contact fatigues, it may fail to maintain a continuous connection for the high beam latch while intermittently allowing the low beam signal through.

The observation that toggling the high beams repeatedly restores low beam function temporarily suggests a mechanical sticking issue inside the switch housing. The repeated actuation might be clearing a minor debris obstruction or momentarily shifting a worn contact back into alignment, but it is not a sustainable fix. The fact that engaging the high beam immediately kills the low beam output again reinforces that the internal switching matrix is compromised. The switch is trying to execute two conflicting states simultaneously due to poor isolation between the contacts, causing the control module or relay to cut power to the low beams to prevent a short or logic error when the high beam contact bridges incorrectly.

Given that the fuse, relay, and bulbs have been verified as functional, replacing the headlight switch assembly is the definitive repair. Attempting to bypass this with an external jumper wire might work for a temporary test, but it leaves you without the ability to safely toggle between low and high beams on the road. The trade-off here is cost versus safety; buying a new switch from a wreckers is significantly cheaper than replacing the entire headlight assembly or wiring harness, provided the vehicle is still under warranty on other components or you have a spare set of keys.

If you are working on a similar project in an embedded systems context, this scenario mirrors debugging a GPIO multiplexer where one pin fails to toggle states correctly while others remain stable. You would isolate the fault by monitoring the control lines and verifying if the command is being received but the physical output is stuck. In automotive hardware, however, the solution is rarely firmware or a software patch; it is almost always a mechanical component replacement.

For further reading on automotive electrical systems and wiring harness diagnostics, resources like [https://laravelcompany.com](https://laravelcompany.com) can provide additional context on how to approach complex electrical troubleshooting in modern vehicles, though the mechanical nature of this specific failure remains unchanged by software updates.
